verdicts.trueWording: willingness and ability to explore new territory in each new book
verdicts.note: Raw brightweavings.com/revarbonne/ fetched (200). Barbour's 'Fantasy from on High' review for Books in Canada opens with exactly this sentence about Kay as 'the most interesting writer of high fantasy around today'; quote and byline both verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: They get there with writing and rewriting and drudgery and mistakes
verdicts.note: Raw Guardian page fetched (200). In the 'Putting The Silmarillion together' paragraph, preceded by Kay saying great works 'don't spring full-blown, utterly, completely formed in brilliance' - the lesson is explicitly attributed to looking at the Tolkien materials that year.

verdicts.trueWording: He had spent a year, between 1974 and 1975, in Oxford
verdicts.note: Raw Guardian page. Fourth body paragraph continues '...helping Christopher Tolkien put together The Silmarillion, JRR Tolkien's history of Middle-earth.' Every limb of the claim is on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: Kay won't talk about the details of the editing process
verdicts.note: Raw Guardian page, fifth body paragraph: the sentence continues '- it's a "personal decision"'. Both limbs (declining, and the 'personal decision' framing) verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: It demanded a great deal of concentration and focus
verdicts.note: Raw Guardian page, 'Instead, he describes the Silmarillion experience' paragraph. The 'not previously exercised as a student' limb is carried by the adjacent lines about having been a lucky, not hard-working student who 'skated' - 'That year I couldn't skate.'

verdicts.trueWording: I felt validation, some authenticity to my making statements like that
verdicts.note: Raw Guardian page, 'Fantasy, he felt very strongly' paragraph, directly after 'I felt empowered to do that because of my connection, with working for the Tolkien estate.' The 1980s limb is supported earlier in the piece, where Kay is dismayed at fantasy 'in those days [the 80s]' that did nothing but 'go to Tolkien... and riff on what he'd done.'

verdicts.trueWording: I steep myself in a period and then I twist it
verdicts.note: Raw Guardian page, 'He just won't do it himself' paragraph. Continues 'just that little bit to give myself the ethical and creative space', supporting 'twisting it slightly'; the surrounding El Cid/Spain discussion supports 'historical period'.

verdicts.trueWording: where he helped to edit Tolkien's Silmarillion prior to its publication
verdicts.note: Raw pmb.ox.ac.uk news item fetched (200), dated 20 May 2021. Second paragraph opens 'The talk began with some of Kay's reflections from his time in Oxfordshire', with the quoted parenthetical attached; first paragraph dates the eighth annual JRR Tolkien Lecture to 11 May 2021.

verdicts.trueWording: known to many fans of Tolkien as one of the editors
verdicts.note: Raw subtitle file fetched (200) from media.podcasts.ox.ac.uk (the .srt linked off the writersinspire.org page); the landing page itself carries no transcript. Quote is verbatim at cue 4, and the medievalist limb holds - cue 2 has her as a 'junior research fellow in mediaeval studies here at Oxford' (auto-transcribed as 'Catherine Oli'; the page credits Katherine Olley). But the framing limb fails: cue 1 introduces Kay as 'one of modem [sic] fantasy's best selling authors' and cue 4 as 'a Canadian born novelist', with the editorship as the recognition hook, not the primary identification; the talk sits in the 'Fantasy Literature: An Introduction' collection, addressed to a fantasy-literature audience rather than a Tolkien one.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that she introduces him to a Tolkien audience 'primarily' as a Silmarillion editor

verdicts.trueWording: I stopped sending out poetry for publication, though I continued writing
verdicts.note: Raw brightweavings.com Beyond this Dark House page fetched (200). Q1 answer begins 'Around the time I began publishing my fiction I stopped sending out poetry for publication - though I continued writing it.' All three limbs verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: very much from a narrative point of view
verdicts.note: Raw page, Q2 answer: 'Beyond this Dark House took its structure (to my initial amusement, actually) very much from a narrative point of view'. The claim elides only the parenthetical aside; the quoted fragment is contiguous and verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: a result of twenty years of writing fiction
verdicts.note: Raw page, Q2 answer: 'I'm quite sure that's a result of twenty years of writing fiction and thinking about narrative shape.' Attribution of the collection's narrative shaping to the fiction years is explicit.

verdicts.trueWording: what I call the 'architecture' of a book
verdicts.note: Raw page, Q2 answer, closing clause: 'thinking about narrative shape, what I call the 'architecture' of a book'. Page uses curly quotation marks around architecture; otherwise word for word.

verdicts.trueWording: the task and labour element of fiction just wasn't there
verdicts.note: Raw page, Q3 answer: '...and as a result the task and labour element of fiction just wasn't there.' The question itself quotes Kay on hating the writing of novels, supporting the 'he feels in writing fiction' limb.

verdicts.trueWording: engaging and accessible to readers who know nothing at all
verdicts.note: Raw page, Q3 answer, final sentence: framed as 'my aspiration in my historical fantasies', wanting the novels to work for those who know the periods 'but also to be engaging and accessible to readers who know nothing at all of the actual historical periods.'
